doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Wynton Marsalis and the Marsalis family in New Orleans
summary: He has known Wynton since boyhood from visits to Ellis Marsalis's home with the Newport All-Stars and supports him.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: lot of these young people now. They’re saying, and I’m applauding and I’m very much supportive of a lot of the things that Wynton Marsalis is doing and accomplishing. He’s been anointed in a special role now. And I’ve known him since he was a little boy because I knew his mother and father and I was at his house when he was just a little whippersnapper going around. Because I was working in New Orleans at the Royal Sonesta Hotel with the Newport All-Stars. And Ellis had myself and Lenny McBrowne, the drummer, to come over to his house and his wife cooked breakfast for us and we sat around and talked. And I’ve known those kids since they were little whippersnappers. Little acorns that grew into big nuts. And Wynton has grown. You know he alienated a lot of people early on because he was very outspoken and quick to be very opinionated. And I think he’s learned a great deal. But that’s the folly of youth sometimes. And then when you’re thrown out there and given so much access to stars and stuff, it can be overwhelming. But people are so quick to want to put him down or this, that and the other. But let’s just bear with the brother. And help him out. And that’s why I spent time with him when we’re around, I go up to his apartment and we hang. And he respects me. And I respect him. And he knows that I respect him. And he has his thoughts and his feelings about things. But I always try to engage him in dialogue. Not talking down to him because I’m older than he. But share ideas. Because it’s about win-win. Life is a constant state of negotiation.
